title: ChOCI-R-S Severity Descriptors
text:
Each score is reported with a severity descriptor. The Total Impairment descriptors use the CY-BOCS severity bands (Goodman et al., 1989), converted to ChOCI-R-S scores using the table of equivalent scores in Uher et al. (2008). The Total Symptoms descriptors sit one standard deviation either side of the clinical mean in the same study. The lowest impairment band, called “subclinical” on the CY-BOCS, is labelled “Minimal” in NovoPsych because the reference sample is children and adolescents attending an OCD clinic.
The descriptors are a descriptive guide, not diagnostic cut-offs, and do not replace clinical judgement. NovoPsych placed each subscale’s cut-offs at the same percentile as the matching Total cut-off, using each subscale’s own mean and SD from Uher et al. (2008), with each band starting at the next whole score. For symptoms, Moderate starts at about the 16th percentile and High at about the 84th. For impairment, Mild starts at about the 1st–2nd percentile, Moderate about the 16th, Severe about the 56th and Extreme about the 90th. The parent-report ChOCI-R-P has different raw-score cut-offs, because each form is converted through its own column of the equivalence table and its own norms, so the same raw score does not mean the same thing on the two forms.
Note. The CY-BOCS severity bands (0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31, 32–40) are widely used and are usually cited to Goodman et al. (1989), and sometimes to the CY-BOCS validation paper (Scahill et al., 1997). NovoPsych could not find them in either paper, in the scale authors’ later work, or anywhere else. We therefore treat them as an established clinical convention, and keep them for consistency with common practice and with earlier NovoPsych reports.

title: How should I interpret a large gap between the child-rated ChOCI-R-S and the parent-rated ChOCI-R-P?
text: Discrepancies between informants are common and the gap itself is useful clinical data. Parents typically have better visibility of observable compulsions (washing, checking, asking for reassurance) and tend to underestimate obsessions and covert rituals. Children may underreport when symptoms feel shameful, when insight is limited (more common in younger children), or when they have learned to mask symptoms in front of caregivers. When the parent score substantially exceeds the child score, consider limited insight, minimisation, or symptom concealment. When the child score exceeds the parent score, suspect covert symptoms or content the child has not disclosed at home. Both perspectives can provide valuable clinical information; the divergence becomes a formulation discussion point and may warrant exploring family accommodation patterns.

title: How should I respond clinically when a young person with elevated ChOCI-R-S scores also presents with anxiety, tics, or attentional difficulties?
text: Co-occurring psychiatric conditions are common in paediatric OCD rather than the exception, with around 74 percent of children meeting criteria for at least one additional disorder (Stiede et al., 2024). Practically, an elevated ChOCI-R-S should prompt considerations of assessment for generalised anxiety, separation anxiety, specific phobias, tic disorders, and ADHD as clinically indicated before finalising a treatment plan. Comorbidity influences sequencing: co-occurring anxiety may require adaptations to treatment planning, tic disorders can blur the line between compulsions and motor/vocal tics on the Compulsion subscale (worth clarifying in interview), and untreated ADHD can undermine engagement with between-session exposure tasks. Documenting which conditions are present, which are driving impairment, and which are likely to interact with CBT-with-ERP is more useful than ChOCI-R-S scores alone.

title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used outside the 7 to 17 year age range?
text: The ChOCI-R-S is intended for children and adolescents aged 7 to 17 years. Use below age 7 is not recommended, as percentile interpretation may be less reliable because the reference distribution does not include this end of the range, and younger children may find a self-report questionnaire hard to complete; the parent-report ChOCI-R-P is a useful alternative. Above age 17, an adult OCD measure such as the OCI-R would typically be more appropriate.

title: How do I use repeat ChOCI-R-S administration to inform session-by-session treatment decisions?
text: For active CBT-with-ERP, ChOCI-R-S administration every week or two may help monitor symptom and impairment changes over time. A declining Compulsion Symptoms score alongside persistently elevated Obsession Symptoms may warrant exploring whether overt rituals are reducing while the underlying obsessional content remains distressing. This suggests the exposure hierarchy may need to shift toward the feared thought rather than the behaviour. A flat or rising Impairment score despite falling Symptoms scores may indicate entrenched family accommodation that has not yet been targeted. Plateaus across several weeks may prompt a hierarchy review and a check on between-session exposure adherence. In maintenance or follow-up, administration frequency can be adjusted according to clinical need, treatment goals, and risk of symptom recurrence.

title: Can the ChOCI-R-S be used to screen for or confirm a diagnosis of OCD?
text: No. The ChOCI-R-S measures OCD symptom content and severity; it is not a diagnostic or screening instrument. It is intended for young people with known or suspected OCD, and its scores are referenced against an OCD-diagnosed sample rather than the general population. Diagnosis should rest on clinical assessment, and where the aim is to detect possible OCD in an unselected group, a dedicated screening measure is more appropriate.

title: Does a low score or a "Minimal" descriptor mean the young person does not have OCD?
text: No. Because the reference sample was made up entirely of young people diagnosed with OCD, scores describe severity relative to that group rather than to the general population. A low percentile or a “Minimal” descriptor therefore means the young person’s reported symptoms or impairment are lower than those of most young people in the OCD clinical reference sample. The measure should not be used to rule OCD in or out.

title: With six scores produced, which should be the main focus for reporting and progress monitoring?
text: Total Impairment is the primary score for most purposes. It reflects overall OCD-related functional disruption and is comparable to the total score of the clinician-administered CY-BOCS, which makes it a useful headline figure and a key metric for tracking progress over the course of treatment. Total Symptoms complements it by capturing the breadth of symptoms endorsed, while the four subscale scores are best used to examine the balance of obsessions and compulsions and identify domain-specific patterns that may be obscured by the total scores.
